BOI.name: Boise
BOI.excerpt: The mid week low pressure system will be on the way out Wednesday, resulting in breezy afternoon winds but little to no precipitation.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Rain and high elevation snow decreasing from west to east today.
- Cooler with gusty winds today and tonight. Near to slightly above normal temperatures through the week.
- Dry Monday through Wednesday, then a slight chance of precipitation late week.

sections.name: Short Term
paragraphs: A Pacific cold front exiting east of the region early this evening will leave a strong post-frontal surface pressure gradient across southern Idaho. Gusty westerly winds will remain the primary impact through late this evening, especially along the Interstate 84 corridor from Mountain Home through the Western Magic Valley. In these areas, sustained winds of 20 to 30 mph with peak gusts reaching 45 mph before winds steadily taper off after midnight as the gradient relaxes and surface decoupling occurs.

Behind the front, scattered shower activity over the central Idaho mountains will diminish overnight, giving way to clearing skies. Patchy valley fog may develop early Monday morning in sheltered basins that received wetting rains, particularly across southeast Oregon and west-central Idaho. However, its unlikely fog will develop across the Snake Plain given sustained winds overnight.

A transitory upper-level ridge builds overhead Monday into Monday night, yielding dry conditions and near-normal daytime temperatures. Mid and high clouds increase on Tuesday ahead of the next weak shortwave trough advancing out of the eastern Pacific. Model guidance keeps the bulk of moisture and upper support split north and south of our forecast area, with precipitation chances limited mainly to isolated showers over the higher terrain of the West Central Mountains late Tuesday and Tuesday night. Temperatures through Tuesday night will remain within a few degrees of seasonal normals.

sections.name: Long Term
paragraphs: The mid week low pressure system will be on the way out Wednesday, resulting in breezy afternoon winds but little to no precipitation. Additional systems will move by to the north on Thursday and Friday, resulting in a 10-30% chance of showers on Thursday and a 20-40% chance on Friday, highest across our northern CWA. Over the weekend, an upper-level ridge is forecast to build with dry conditions returning. The weak systems Wednesday through Friday will bring slight cooling, but temperatures will still be near normal. Slightly warmer temperatures will arrive over the weekend as the ridge builds in.

BOU.name: Boulder / Denver
BOU.excerpt: By the weekend, there could be another cold front cooling temperatures down as hinted in the ECMWF AI ensembles.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Snow likely (> 80% chance) for the mountains through most of Monday. Snow level falls to 9,000 to 9,500 feet Monday morning and down to 8,000 feet Monday afternoon.
- Mountain roads will become slippery in spots above 8,500 feet, especially through mountain passes.
- Scattered to numerous rain showers and cooler temperatures for the plains on Monday. A few snowflakes possible for the Palmer Divide on Monday night.
- Another chance for some rain and snow for the mountains on Wednesday bringing light precipitation amounts.

sections.name: Discussion
paragraphs: The next storm system has started to affect our area over the last few hours with some light rain/snow showers across the high country and light rain showers for the majority of the plains. Some light rain/snow showers continue at this hour for the Medicine Bow Range and light rain showers for the far northeastern plains. With the saturated grounds from the Sunday evening rain, fog is possible once again. Favored locations look to be northern Colorado and possibly extending into the northern metro and east to DIA. Have held off on any highlights given the uncertainty with how widespread any fog would be, but an advisory may be needed if confidence increases overnight. Any fog would quickly lift as the cold front moves through on Monday morning.

The trough that will affect our weather over the next 24-36 hours is currently centered over the Great Basin and should quickly push through Colorado by late Monday. Good moisture continues to advect into our area with southwest flow in the mid and upper levels. We expect coverage of precipitation to increase by Monday morning through the early afternoon as lift increases and the cold front pushes through from north to south. The cold front moves through the metro around 6-9am and looks to clear our area by about 2pm Monday. In its wake, afternoon temperatures should struggle to make it out of the upper 40s for much of the plains given the clouds in place and the chance for showers. Some scattered showers could linger on the plains through Tuesday morning with some upslope continuing.

QPF is very similar to the last forecast package. Ensemble guidance continues to coalesce on 0.1-0.4" rainfall for the Denver metro with some locally higher amounts possible mainly for the southeast portions of the metro. Similar rainfall totals look possible for most of the plains with some signal that western Washington County and adjacent areas could see the most rainfall. This is likely due to a rather deep upslope component (northerly winds) from the surface up to 500 mb behind the cold front. For the northern high country, many areas should see 0.50-0.75" QPF with some higher amounts possible. Lesser amounts are expected for the rest of the high country.

As for snow, snow showers will start to increase in coverage over the next few hours for the high country. Colder air will continue to filter in aloft quickly lowering snow levels. Snow levels are currently around 10,500 feet, but quickly drop through the overnight to around 9,250 feet by Monday morning. Snow levels will continue to drop to near 7,500-8,000 feet or even a bit lower by Monday evening. The Palmer Divide still has a chance for some snowflakes to mix in on Monday evening as precipitation chances start to wind down. The Winter Weather Advisory goes into effect early this morning and lasts through late Monday night. The forecast remains on track with 3-8 inches of snowfall expected in general. As previously noted, northerly flow is expected as the trough pushes through. In this flow pattern, the northern mountains continue to look most favored in our area for the highest snowfall totals with some totals greater than 9 inches possible, particularly at the highest elevations. DESI probabilities highlight this potential well with a 50% chance or greater of snowfall totals exceeding 6 inches for the Park Range, northern Gore Range, and Medicine Bow Range. Note that higher totals are still possible for areas along the Front Range Mountains including Summit County and RMNP, but much less likely.

Monday and even Tuesday will also feature some breezy conditions for the plains. DESI probabilities show at least a 40% chance for wind gusts exceeding 55 mph on Monday afternoon and evening across our plains. Given the lack of subsidence and momentum transfer, we have held off on any wind highlights. Most locations on the plains should see gusts of 35-55 mph with isolated locations having the potential for gusts of 55-60 mph Monday afternoon, evening, and into early Tuesday. Wind gusts could still reach 40-50 mph for the far eastern plains on Tuesday afternoon.

After the passage of the trough late Monday into early Tuesday, ridging quickly looks to take its place. Tuesday will be a warmer day with high temperatures near average for this time of year- in the upper 50s. High temperatures should stay near average for the rest of the week. Another low looks to track through our area on Wednesday. The majority of models bring the chance for another round of light snow showers for the high country and possibly some rain showers for the plains. Any accumulation continues to look rather unimpressive with this system at this time. Thursday and Friday should be dry with westerly flow aloft and near-normal temperatures.

By the weekend, there could be another cold front cooling temperatures down as hinted in the ECMWF AI ensembles. Other ensemble guidance keeps high temperatures in the upper 50s and possibly warming into the low 60s for the plains on the back half of the weekend. A trough could graze us to the east putting us in the right exit region of the jet- where subsidence is favored. Therefore, regardless of the temperatures, the weekend is trending drier.

CYS.name: Cheyenne
CYS.excerpt: Now, switching gears and taking a closer look at temperatures for the long term period, expect highs to climb into the mid to upper 40s, possibly a few location topping out in the lower 50s, west of I- 25.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - A complex but disorganized storm system will move into the area Sunday, bringing multiple rounds of rain and snow showers through Tuesday morning.
- Winter Weather Advisories are in place for the mountains as well as the Arlington area and South Laramie Range. Accumulating heavy, wet snow is possible in these areas.
- Widespread windy conditions are anticipated Monday and Monday night.

sections.name: Short Term
paragraphs: Currently looking at a dreary day across most of the forecast area. A blanket of cloud cover sits over the CWA with patchy fog dotting southeast Wyoming and the Nebraska panhandle. Radar does show some light echoes as well, however its hard to confirm whether or not any precipitation is currently making it to the ground. Temperatures are a bit cooler than anticipated, mainly due to the thick cloud cover and lingering fog. But, warm air advection still persists with moist southerly flow keeping 700 mb temperatures on the mild side. Precipitation coverage will increase this evening and overnight, but will likely still be on the spotty side until the system becomes more organized. The cold front will arrive Sunday night, gradually ushering in cooler air. Simultaneously, leeside cyclogenesis will be occurring in northeast Colorado, forming a surface low. Cluster analysis from both the GEFS and ECMWF ensemble are still in good agreement regarding surface low placement and track into the day Monday. A majority of the precipitation that falls overnight will be rain as cooler air slowly fills in behind the front. The exception to this, of course, will be the mountains. Winter Weather Advisories are in place for the Snowy and Sierra Madre Range starting tonight. Snow will begin later this evening and continue through the day Monday. At the end of the event, locations above 9000 feet will likely pick up between 6 and 12 inches.

A colder day is expected Monday behind the front with temperatures in the 30s and 40s for southeast Wyoming and low 50s for the Nebraska panhandle. As a result, snow could begin to mix with rain as snow levels drop to about 5500 feet. The mix and potential full change-over to snow could happen as early as Monday morning for locations along and west of the Laramie Range. PWATs are at climatological max per NAEFS and more closely resemble that of a summer monsoon event! As a result, expect fairly good precipitation rates, especially with Hi-Res guidance showing steady and widespread precipitation once the CWA enters the wrap around moisture regime of the surface low ejecting into Nebraska. Higher precipitation rates could lead to a quicker change over to snow, and thus the potential for higher snowfall accumulations. The mountains and higher elevations are still the areas with the highest confidence in seeing accumulations. Winter Weather Advisories are also in effect for the North Laramie Range, whose northern slopes could see between 6 and 12 inches from upslope flow, and the Arlington area and South Laramie Range. These higher elevation spots along Interstate 80 could pick up roughly 2 to 4 inches of heavy wet snow given the temperatures and PWATs. This could lead to difficult travel at times. Areas outside of the aforementioned locations west of the Laramie Range could also see accumulating snow ranging anywhere from a trace to 2 inches. Snow amounts are a bit more uncertain east of the Laramie Range as the transition may or may not happen later in the day. Hi-Res guidance shows steady precipitation in this area during the afternoon and into the evening hours. Places like Cheyenne and Douglas could see some minor accumulations, but even this is uncertain. Ensemble guidance from both the GFS and ECMWF show very few members with even light accumulations for these cities. The other area to watch will be the Pine Ridge. The HRRR is really latching onto the upslope flow and nails the Pine Ridge between Lusk and Chadron with fairly high accumulations. This is even more uncertain, but lingering precipitation Monday night combined with the north winds could lead to quickly accumulating snow.

The other issue Monday will be the strong winds. As the surface low ejects into Nebraska, a strong MSLP gradient will set up on the eastern plains. Hi-Res guidance like the HRRR suggests marginally high winds east of the Laramie with gusts up to 60 MPH. However, given a lack of any decent subsidence, its hard to rationalize that widespread 60 MPH winds will materialize Monday afternoon into Monday evening. Even NBM probabilities of wind gusts >48 kts are on the low side across the plains. For now, held off on any high wind headlines to allow for a few model cycles to see if there is greater confidence in wind gusts. Regardless, it will be windy on Monday, with frequent gusts of 50 to 55 MPH. These blustery conditions will continue into Tuesday morning, before weakening during the afternoon hours.

The weather on Tuesday looks quieter as the surface low pushes further off to the northeast. Some lingering precipitation and wind will still be present in the Nebraska panhandle during the morning hours, but will taper off by the afternoon. Decreasing clouds are expected throughout the day with mostly sunny skies anticipated by the afternoon. Upper-level ridging will quickly move in behind the storm system, leading to warmer temperatures as 700 mb temperatures rise back into the single digits. Highs in the 40s and 50s are likely, however, could be cooler based on amount of snow cover.

sections.name: Long Term
paragraphs: As we start off the long term period, lets take a quick look at the synoptic setup, we have a deep trough draped south across the Central Plains, just to our east, while ridging builds in from the west. This ridge will keep us in a dry northerly to northeasterly flow regime across our CWA with plentiful sunshine making a triumphant return. As we progress into Wednesday, weak ridging is in place overhead while model consensus has another cut-off low diving southeast from Idaho. This feature will bring an increase chance of precipitation primarily across the Sierra Madre and Snowy Ranges. Where at the higher elevations could get and inch or two of fresh snow. Otherwise, for the remainder of the CWA, this system will not have any impacts elsewhere as it continues to dive southeast across the Four Corners region through Wednesday. Quickly behind it, ridging nudges back in late Wednesday into Thursday. By the tail end of the week into next weekend, there are some differences in model solutions with the placement and amplitude of synoptic features. With the ECMWF having a deep trough just to our east while the GFS has the trough slightly further east over the Great Lakes. However, most model solutions have a ridge in place over our region with dry northwesterly flow. With all that being said, stay tuned to the forecast for future updates.

Now, switching gears and taking a closer look at temperatures for the long term period, expect highs to climb into the mid to upper 40s, possibly a few location topping out in the lower 50s, west of I- 25. While temperatures will soar into the lower to mid 50s east of I- 25 for the remainder of the work week into the weekend. In general, expect lows to dip into the lower to mid 30s across the CWA, possibly slightly colder west of the I-25 corridor.

GJT.name: Grand Junction
GJT.excerpt: Drier conditions return Tuesday and temperatures will also continue to hover below normal for the better half of the work week.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Several rivers across SW Colorado are forecast to crest overnight Sunday into Monday.
- The San Juan River at Pagosa Springs is forecast to reach major flood stage which has prompted the continuation of the Particularly Dangerous Situation Flood Warning for that area.
- A cold frontal passage will occur overnight Sunday into Monday, driving mountain snowfall at and above pass level. Morning commutes could be slick and slushy.
- Widespread precipitation chances diminish Monday morning, with drier conditions expected Tuesday.

sections.name: Discussion
paragraphs: A cold front pushing across eastern Utah and western Colorado tonight will usher in a cooler air mass, holding temperatures below the seasonal averages to kick off the workweek.

Widespread precipitation will continue across the region overnight before tapering off from southwest to northeast Monday afternoon and evening. An additional 0.5-1" of rainfall remains possible across the higher terrain of the San Juans and adjacent valley basin through early Monday. With snow levels dropping behind the front, snow across the high passes will lead to slick and slushy travel during the Monday morning commute. In the northern Divide mountains, ensemble and deterministic guidance consistently depict 4 to 8 inches of accumulation above 9000 ft. through Monday evening; consequently, the Winter Weather Advisory has been expanded northward to account for these localized travel impacts.

Hydrologic impacts will peak during the overnight hours into Monday morning as area rivers approach crest levels. While precipitation chances diminish late Monday, rivers will remain near or above bankfull well after the rain ceases. Please refer to the hydrology section below for specific river stage and crest forecast information.

Drier conditions return Tuesday and temperatures will also continue to hover below normal for the better half of the work week. A quick moving clipper system has the potential to bring some light showers to the region mid to late next week, although models don't have the best grasp on this as of yet, so details remain vague.

PUB.name: Pueblo
PUB.excerpt: After a drier/warmer day on Tue, most model solutions have latched onto some weak energy sliding through the Rockies Wed/Thu, generating low elevation rain/mtn snow showers across the region especially Wed/Wed night.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Heavy rainfall will continue across the ern San Juans into the evening, with significant and dangerous flooding expected from the mountains downstream into the western edge of the San Luis Valley.
- Snow level finally drops late tonight, with several inches of snow above 9000 feet in the San Juans before precip ends Monday.

- Runoff from heavy rain today and tonight will likely cause flooding along the Rio Grande from Mon-Wed, especially from South Fork downstream to Alamosa. Flooding is also likely along the Conejos River.
- Dry and warmer on Tue, then a weak weather system will bring a chance of showers to much of the region Wed into early Thu.

sections.name: Short Term
paragraphs: After a bit of a lull in precip rates around midday, early afternoon observations and radar data suggest rainfall is increasing in coverage and intensity this afternoon over the San Juans and adjacent areas, with snow level climbing toward 11k feet across the area. Most CAMs suggest period from now (2pm MST) until around 10 pm will see the heaviest rainfall, with additional QPF of over 2 inches possible by midnight, then rain changes to snow above 9000 feet and rates decrease by sunrise on Mon. Combo of snow and wind could make for difficult travel over Wolf Creek and Cumbres Passes Mon morning, with Winter Storm Warning in effect until midday Mon. Overall, current set of flood highlights for the area look in good shape, but expect we'll see multiple areal/river flood warnings later today and tonight, as run-off hits area waterways and heads downstream. Elsewhere, scattered showers expected to continue over the higher terrain this afternoon and evening, with perhaps a few quick moving showers/thunderstorms on the plains this evening, before downslope drying ends most activity along/east of the mountains and across the plains after midnight.

On Monday, upper low moves through Colorado, with strong surface cold front sweeping southward through the plains during the late morning hours. Over the mountains, switch to more west and eventually northwest upper flow should decrease precip intensity/coverage over the San Juans through the morning, while snow picks up in the central mountains as snow levels fall and upward motion increases. Higher elevations from Monarch Pass northward could see a few inches of snow and some blowing/drifting by afternoon, though accumulations look low enough to preclude issuance of an advisory at this point. Over the eastern mountains and plains, strong north winds will develop by afternoon behind the cold front, with enough upward motion for fairly widespread showers/isolated thunderstorms from early afternoon into early evening, though focus for precip will shift toward the NM border/srn I-25 corridor fairly quickly as precip hole develops over COS/PUB (though 18z HRRR has a bullseye of heavier precip over COS/PUB around noon before activity shifts south). Could get cold enough for some snow showers along the Palmer Divide Mon evening before lift exits the area into the plains by midnight.

sections.name: Long Term
paragraphs: After a drier/warmer day on Tue, most model solutions have latched onto some weak energy sliding through the Rockies Wed/Thu, generating low elevation rain/mtn snow showers across the region especially Wed/Wed night. Still not expecting heavy precip as system continues to look moisture-starved, though some light snow accumulations over the higher mountains look possible. End of the week/weekend upper trough position continues to shift east, suggesting most impacts and precip will be east of the area, though associated cold front may bring some brief light sprinkles and cooler temperatures to the region on Fri.

SLC.name: Salt Lake City
SLC.excerpt: Ensemble guidance has come into better agreement with a weak mid- level trough sweeping through the Great Basin on Wednesday.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Accumulating mountain snow is expected across all Utah mountains through Monday morning. Upwards of 12" of snow is expected above 9000 feet, and 3-6" of snow down to around 7000 feet. Upper elevations of the Cottonwoods and western Uintas may see localized accumulations 18-24".
- Cool, dry, and stable conditions build in Tuesday following the passage of this system.
- A weak system looks to impact the region Wednesday/Thursday ushering in a brief period of low elevation rainfall and high elevation snowfall across primarily northern and central Utah.

sections.name: Discussion
paragraphs: Currently, a mid-level trough is traversing across the Great Basin with its axis nearly centered along the UT/NV border. With this trough, a cold front continues to sweep across much of UT, having already traversed the western half of the state. While the lower levels are slowly drying out, weak ascent with modest moisture aloft will result in light to occasionally moderate rainfall persisting across much of the forecast area through roughly 09z. From 09z on, higher terrain will be favored for precipitation given drier low levels of the atmosphere. As such, the flood watch will be allowed to expire at 06z for southern UT and portions of central UT.

700mb temperatures will continue to cool following the passage of the cold front to roughly -3C to -4C resulting in snow levels continuing to drop through the evening to around 6500ft. Additionally, northwest flow aloft will persist, resulting in a favorable pattern for widespread mountain snow across much of Utah's high terrain. Of note, a TROWAL feature has been identified via satellite imagery serving to wrap more moisture around the northwest side of a deepening upper low located over northern UT. This has resulted in another round of widespread light to moderate rain observed across northern UT, and will also contribute to snowfall totals across our northern UT mountains. Across our UT high terrain (generally 9000ft or greater), 3-6" of additional snowfall is expected. Some areas, such as the Upper Cottonwoods and Western Uintas may see additional snowfall totals from 6-12" given favorable northwest flow orientation overnight.

Transient ridging builds in Monday in the wake of the deepening trough as it progresses east. This will result in most precipitation coming to a halt across the forecast area, though some lingering showers across the UT high terrain may persist. This feature is forecast to persist through Tuesday bringing quiescent conditions and unseasonably cool temperatures, potentially as low a 15F below seasonal normals areawide.

Ensemble guidance has come into better agreement with a weak mid- level trough sweeping through the Great Basin on Wednesday. This system is not expected to bring a whole lot of moisture with it, and with weak forcing, only light valley rainfall with light mountain snow accumulations are expected across northern and central UT. Following this system, dry conditions develop once again as ridging becomes dominant across much of the western U.S. through the remainder of the week and into the weekend.

2660.travel_advice: Very dangerous avalanche conditions. Travel in avalanche terrain not recommended.

product.author: Krista Beyer
bottom_line: A Special Avalanche Advisory is in effect for the San Juan Mountains and the La Plata Mountains.

A potent winter storm increases avalanche hazard through Monday evening. Rain, snow, and wind impacts will rapidly change avalanche conditions. Upper elevations may see two feet of new snow, creating dangerous avalanche conditions above treeline. Stay out from under large connected alpine slopes, as avalanches can break wider and travel farther than expected.

2701.travel_advice: Heightened avalanche conditions on specific terrain features. Evaluate snow and terrain carefully; identify features of concern.

product.author: Ian Fowler
bottom_line: New snow and strong overnight winds increase avalanche danger. The most hazardous slopes are where the new snow falls on old-firm or faceted surfaces from October storms. High-elevation shady slopes are most likely to have this combination. If you find snow that cracks avoid steep slopes.

2842.travel_advice: Watch for signs of unstable snow such as recent avalanches, cracking in the snow, and audible collapsing. Avoid traveling on or under similar slopes.

product.author: Kevin Studley
hazard_discussion: Avalanche Forecasting Operations Have Come to a Close for the 2026-26 Season
Have a safe spring in the mountains. Continue to remain vigilant and flexible while traveling in the mountains this spring.
OBSERVATIONS

Observations are still greatly appreciated. Spring-time observations are extremely helpful as forecast operations have come to a close. If you're out in the mountains, submit an observation to let the rest of the public know what's going on out there. Even a simple weather observation can be very useful.
• View recent observations HERE
• Submit an observation HERE
• Recent photos and videos HERE
Snow and Avalanche Information
• Dry Slab avalanche problems such as storm slab and wind slab avalanches are most likely during and immediately following a storm.

• Wet Loose avalanches are expected during warmups and (even brief) clear, sunny weather events, and rain events. Watch for pinwheels and rollerballs as an indicator the snow is becoming damp. If you're sinking into soft, mushy snow, it's time to turn around or find a different aspect.

• Wet Slab avalanches become likely during rain events and with multiple nights above freezing. Wet slabs occur when melt water pools and lubricates crusts or older persistent weak layers. Wet slab avalanches are notoriously difficult to predict.
• Cornices are large and often become unstable during prolonged warmups. Give yourself plenty of space above and below them. They tend to begin shedding during warming and/or rain events.
• Dry Loose Snow avalanches are expected during and immediately after a storm, particularly on shaded, north-facing slopes.

• Glide avalanches typically fail in similar spots year after year after an abundance of meltwater has saturated the ground or lower snowpack. Glide avalanches can occur in steep terrain, on smooth grassy slopes or on large slabs of rock. Look for glide cracks opening up during spring.
WEATHER
• Click HERE to view our Weather Station Map page with updated webcams
• Click HERE to view our Weather Tools page
• Spring weather patterns are often erratic and snow conditions can change quickly during spring weather. Be attentive to these changes and remain flexible with your travel plans.
• Rain on snow events can create dangerous avalanche conditions in a short period of time.
• Spring time means a higher sun angle, with direct solar radiation on the snowpack. Even a brief dose of sunshine can quickly alter the snow surface.

• Overcast skies and snow showers can open up to full sunshine in a matter of minutes. Convective snow showers can be spotty and difficult to forecast. Temperatures can vary depending on elevation and unexpected cloud cover can significantly alter a weather forecast.
OTHER CONSIDERATIONS
• Travel
• As people push into steeper, more consequential terrain, remember to maintain safe travel protocols and not let your guard down just because it's sunny and warm.
• During melt-freeze cycles, pay attention to "slide-for-life" circumstances, particularly during morning travel.
• Be mindful of terrain selection and timing. Identify terrain traps and be prepared to avoid/manage them.
• Spring Mindset

• Springtime is when mountain travelers push for bigger objectives. We have greater confidence in the stability of the snowpack and the high sun angle makes us feel ready to charge. As we start stepping out into bigger terrain in the mountains, be mindful of consequences (ask yourself, "If this slides, what will happen?"). Choose your terrain appropriately and manage new/surface snow problems accordingly. Be aware that dynamic weather can have quick impacts on the snow surface. A common theme I've noticed over the last 15 years playing in steep, snowy mountains is that experienced, seasoned people often get caught in small avalanches in big terrain during the spring. We have a tendency to underestimate "manageable" new snow problems like wind slab and loose snow. Pay attention to changing weather and know that small shifts in spring weather can have dramatic impacts on the upper snowpack.
Seasonal SNOW AND PRECIPITATION Comparison
(Precipitation data are recorded from Secesh SNOTEL site at 6540')

• December - 68" (12.6" SWE)
• January - 37" (5.1" SWE)
• February - 41" (5.4" SWE)
• March - 24" (5.2" SWE) Peak Height of Snow - 70" (03/05)

2755.travel_advice: Generally safe avalanche conditions. Watch for unstable snow on isolated terrain features.

product.author: Ian Fowler
bottom_line: Most slopes lack enough snow to produce an avalanche. If you find a steep slope with firm, continuous snow close to ridges, go around it to avoid the hazard. You find this hazard at high elevations.

2735.travel_advice: Heightened avalanche conditions on specific terrain features. Evaluate snow and terrain carefully; identify features of concern.

product.author: Ian Fowler
bottom_line: Most slopes are safe to travel on as they have very little snow. On high-elevation north-, northeast-, and east-facing slopes, if you find firm, hollow snow, you could trigger an avalanche. If in doubt, just walk around these drifts of snow.
